Battle
BAT-'l
n. (rendering Hebrew milchāmâh and Greek polemos, parataxis)
From Old French bataille, from Late Latin battualia, fencing exercises, from battuere, to beat. A battle is properly the single engagement, as distinguished from the war of which it is a part — and the Authorized Version keeps that distinction reasonably well, using battle for the day of engagement and the array of troops (as in the horse is prepared against the day of battle).

Biblical Definition

Scripture's doctrine of battle is stated in one sentence by a boy with a sling: “the battle is the LORD'S, and he will give you into our hands” (1Sa 17:47), and David says it after declaring that the LORD saveth not with sword and spear. The lesson is repeated to a whole kingdom by Jahaziel in Jehoshaphat's crisis: “Be not afraid nor dismayed by reason of this great multitude; for the battle is not yours, but God's” (2Ch 20:15) — and Judah went out with singers before the army. The doctrine does not abolish preparation; it puts preparation in its place. Solomon states the balance exactly: “The horse is prepared against the day of battle: but safety is of the LORD” (Pro 21:31). The horse is to be prepared — the proverb assumes it — and the outcome still belongs to God, which is neither fatalism nor self-reliance but the ordinary Reformed account of means under providence. The title that gathers it all is in the psalm of the ascending King: “Who is this King of glory? The LORD strong and mighty, the LORD mighty in battle” (Psa 24:8). The New Testament transposes the whole vocabulary without softening it: the Christian's day of battle is the evil day, his array is the whole armour of God, and his victory is already secured by a Lord who spoiled principalities and powers and triumphed over them openly.

Webster 1828 Definition

A single armed engagement; in Scripture the appointed occasion on which it is shewn that safety is of the LORD — the horse prepared and the outcome God's — and the source of the divine title, the LORD mighty in battle.

expand to see more

BATTLE, n. 1. A fight, or encounter between enemies, or opposing armies; an engagement.

2. A body of forces, or division of an army, drawn up in array. The battle of the Israelites was set in array against the Philistines.

3. In Scripture, the day of battle is the day of trial and of deliverance, in which it is made manifest that the LORD saveth not with sword and spear. 1 Sam. 17.

4. To join battle; to meet in hostile encounter. To give battle; to attack an enemy.

5. The LORD mighty in battle; a title of Jehovah as the deliverer and King of glory. Psalm 24.

Key Scripture

1 Samuel 17:47 — "And all this assembly shall know that the LORD saveth not with sword and spear: for the battle is the LORD'S, and he will give you into our hands."

2 Chronicles 20:15 — "And he said, Hearken ye, all Judah, and ye inhabitants of Jerusalem, and thou king Jehoshaphat, Thus saith the LORD unto you, Be not afraid nor dismayed by reason of this great multitude; for the battle is not yours, but God's."

Proverbs 21:31 — "The horse is prepared against the day of battle: but safety is of the LORD."

Psalm 24:8 — "Who is this King of glory? The LORD strong and mighty, the LORD mighty in battle."

Modern Corruption

“The battle is the LORD's” is used to excuse the neglect of ordinary means, as though preparation were unbelief; and in the other direction the language of spiritual battle is used to dramatise personal difficulties until every inconvenience becomes warfare.

expand to see more

The passivity error takes 2Ch 20:15 as a rule against effort. But even in that chapter Judah was told to go down against them and to set themselves and stand still; they marched, they arrayed, and they went in order. David ran toward the Philistine, and he had chosen five smooth stones out of the brook. Pro 21:31 is the settled statement of the principle: the horse is prepared, and safety is of the LORD. Reformed theology has always insisted that God ordains the means along with the end, so that trusting providence is a reason for diligence rather than a substitute for it. The man who will not prepare the horse is not trusting God; he is tempting Him.

The opposite inflation is now common in devotional speech, where every setback is called a battle, every critic an enemy, and every difficulty spiritual warfare, until the vocabulary is worn out and cannot be used when a real conflict comes. Scripture is more sober. It names the actual enemies — principalities, powers, the rulers of the darkness of this world, spiritual wickedness in high places — and it names the actual weapons, which are truth, righteousness, the gospel of peace, faith, salvation, the word of God, and prayer. Nothing in that list is a technique for winning arguments or removing inconveniences, and a Christian who has learned to call his irritations warfare will be poorly equipped when the evil day actually arrives.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew uses the same word for war and battle, milchāmâh, with ma'ārākâh for the battle array or line drawn up. Greek polemos is the conflict; parataxis, the drawing up in order, lies behind the military imagery of the epistles.

expand to see more

Hebrew milchāmâh (H4421) — war, battle, the engagement itself; the word of the battle is the LORD'S in 1Sa 17:47.

Hebrew ma'ārākâh (H4634) — a rank or row, an army set in array; used repeatedly in the Goliath narrative of the armies drawn up against each other.

Hebrew tsābā' (H6635) — host, army, service; the divine title LORD of hosts is a battle title before it is anything else.

Greek polemos (G4171) — war, battle; used of the battle of that great day of God Almighty (Rev 16:14).

Greek panoplia (G3833) — the full armour of a heavy infantryman; the word of Eph 6:11, the whole armour of God, presupposing a day of battle.

Usage

"Of the LORD's ownership of the outcome: the battle is the LORD'S (1Sa 17:47); the battle is not yours, but God's (2Ch 20:15)."

"Of means and providence together: the horse is prepared against the day of battle: but safety is of the LORD (Pro 21:31)."

"Of the divine warrior and the last conflict: the LORD mighty in battle (Psa 24:8); gather them to the battle of that great day (Rev 16:14)."
